newsitem.title: GERMANY: Floods displace east Germans, loom anew in Poland.
newsitem.headline: Floods displace east Germans, loom anew in Poland.

text.p: Thousands of German soldiers fought to contain the rain-gorged Oder River on Friday as authorities ordered reluctant residents to evacuate.

Eastern Germany was suffering a downstream sequel to the disastrous flooding that hit two neighbouring countries earlier this month while Poland braced for another high water surge with more rain forecast this weekend.
The Oder punctured two major dikes and submerged two villages as German soldiers mounted their biggest peacetime operation since World War Two to save more communities from watery doom.

Some 1,500 border guards pitched in with 65 helicopters and 100 boats and another 5,400 soldiers raced to reinforce beleaguered dikes protecting a low-lying strip along the Oder, which forms part of the German-Polish border.

Officials predicted disaster if dikes gave way in the Oderbruch region north of Frankfurt an der Oder, an area which was drained and turned into farmland 250 years ago and protected from the Oder by man-made dikes.

"We have no idea when this catastrophe will be over," Manfred Stolpe, premier of Brandenburg state told a news conference, calling the flooding the worst to hit the region in more than a thousand years.

The 250 sq-km (150 sq mile) Oderbruch region, including the regional town of Bad Freienwalde, faced inundation within hours if one sagging dike collapsed. About 1,000 helpers were struggling to hold it up.
Local television broadcast messages telling 5,000 residents in around 17 villages to start evacuating after officials decided the Hohenwutzen dike could give way.
Trucks carrying sheep and cattle rolled out of the area, a fertile plain growing grains, vegetables and sunflowers that was the breadbasket of the former communist East Germany.
Authorities estimated virtually all of the Oderbruch's 20,000 inhabitants might have to leave if the dike burst.
South of Frankfurt an der Oder, officials said about 3,000 people in the villages of Ziltendorf and Wiesenau would have to leave as a result of a dike breach.
Evacuations were sluggish in the early going as residents were reluctant to abandon their homes, belongings and livestock.

Torrential rain over east-central Europe earlier this month unleashed flooding that killed more than 100 people in Poland and the Czech Republic, where some of eastern Germany's larger waterways originate.
In Poland, weather forecasters expected another round of rain that could re-swell the Odra River, as the Oder is known in that country.

"We don't expect the water to spill over flood protection dikes, but there is danger because they are so eroded by this three-week soaking that something could happen," Polish crisis committee spokesman Krzysztof Pomes said.

The forecast was a blow to thousands of troops and volunteers labouring with sandbags at key points along the river to prevent the mushy dikes from bursting under the strain of high water swells prompted by rain last weekend.
